issues.failure_explanation: The proof invokes a rational-independence argument that requires the values y_{j_p}=ψ_q(c_q^{j_p}) to be rational. However, ψ_q(c_q^{j_p})=j_p·h+(h+δ^μ)/2−φ((1−q)δ), and φ((1−q)δ)=(h−δ^μ)(P((N−q)/(N−1))−1). Since μ is a free real parameter, δ^μ is generically irrational, so the y-values lie in Q(δ^μ) (a degree-2 extension of Q), not in Q. The quoted Lorentz Lemma 2.1 is also garbled and its hypotheses are not met. The rational-independence argument therefore does not apply, and the distinctness claim is unproved.

for all $-1\le k\le J-1,$ and fixed  $ j_l\in \{-1,\ldots, J-1\}$ with $l\not=p.$  Then we interpolate   $\big\{(t_k, s_k)\big\}_{k=-1}^{J-1}$  using the smeared-out Heaviside function $S$

issues.failure_explanation: The proof bounds the interpolation error by |s_{k+1}−s_k| ≤ C_α(Nδ)^α/N, which requires that consecutive data points in the S-interpolation (sorted by τ=a_q^j) are row-neighbors at distance h in x-space. This ordering is guaranteed only by the (lambdaPQ) condition (Lemma SprecherLambda). For general rationally independent λ not satisfying (lambdaPQ), rows interlace: consecutive sorted points can be from different rows and O(1) apart in x-space, giving |s_{k+1}−s_k| ≤ O(1/N) instead of O((Nδ)^α/N). Summed over N levels, the total error becomes O(1), destroying the convergence. Moreover, the outer function g_q is constructed by gluing row-interpolations on [0,|λ|₁], which requires non-overlapping row τ-ranges—again only guaranteed by (lambdaPQ). Thus the construction itself is not well-defined for the rationally independent case as stated.

The numerical result may be faster than the theoretical bound, but it is not what the theorem predicts.
